lesson.explanationSimple: The Pythagorean theorem only works in a right triangle — a triangle with a 90° angle. The longest side, opposite the right angle, is called the hypotenuse. The theorem says: the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. So if triangle ABC has its right angle at A: BC² = AB² + AC². For example, if AB = 3 and AC = 4, then BC² = 9 + 16 = 25, so BC = 5.
lesson.explanationFormal: Pythagorean theorem: if triangle ABC is right-angled at A, then the square of the length of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides: BC² = AB² + AC². It is used to compute an unknown side of a right triangle when the other two sides are known. Note: the converse of the theorem is used to prove that a triangle is right-angled.
steps: Check that the triangle is right-angled and locate the right angle.
Identify the hypotenuse: the side opposite the right angle (the longest side).
Write the relation: hypotenuse² = first side² + second side².
Take the square root to find the length.
